JMPR: Malathion
EU:
Reg. 396/2005: Malathion (sum of malathion and malaoxon expressed as malathion)
Peer review (EFSA, 2009c): Malathion and malaoxon
efsa_comments:
JMPR 2025 assessed malathion metabolism studies in alfalfa, cotton, lettuce, wheat (foliar and post‐harvest), apples and rice. In primary crops, metabolism mainly proceeded through de‐esterification to mono‐ and dicarboxylic acids, followed by incorporation into natural products. Parent malathion was the major residue component, whereas the more toxicologically potent malaoxon occurred at lower levels, with malaoxon‐to‐malathion ratios ranging from not detected in stored wheat grain to 23% TRR in apples. Minor metabolites included desmethyl‐malathion and related carboxylic acids.
For rotational crops, a confined study conducted at approximately 2N showed decreasing residues with increasing plant back intervals, with the lowest residues at 365 DAA. At 30 DAA, only parent malathion was identified in lettuce, turnip and wheat at low levels (0.02–0.03 mg/kg; 11%–20% TRR), while malaoxon was not detected. Residue transfer to rotational crops is not expected at GAP compliant use.
In livestock, metabolism studies in goats and laying hens showed rapid metabolism of malathion. Parent malathion was not detected in tissues, milk or eggs; residues were mainly present as low‐level polar metabolites and were not considered fat soluble.
JMPR proposed malathion as the residue definition for enforcement in plant products. For dietary risk assessment, JMPR considered the sum of malathion and 30 × malaoxon appropriate, reflecting the higher toxicological potency of malaoxon. However, the residue definition for risk assessment was not finalised, mainly due to the lack of toxicological information for metabolites formed under sterilisation conditions, in particular monoethyl fumarate and mercaptosuccinate.
For the metabolites tetraethyl dithiosuccinate, diethyl methylthiosuccinate and M18, limited toxicological information was available. JMPR, therefore, applied the TTC approach for Cramer class III compounds and did not include these metabolites in the residue definition for risk assessment. For monoethyl maleate, diethyl maleate and diethyl fumarate, a genotoxic potential could not be excluded (see Table on HBGVs); JMPR, therefore, applied the TTC for genotoxicity and did not include these compounds in the residue definition for risk assessment.
At EU level, the enforcement residue definition for plant and animal products is the sum of malathion and malaoxon, expressed as malathion. In the peer review, malathion and malaoxon were proposed for enforcement in plants, while no specific residue definition for animal products was required for the representative uses assessed. For risk assessment in plants, the EU residue definition includes malathion, malaoxon, desmethyl‐malathion, malathion monocarboxylic acid and malathion dicarboxylic acid, expressed as malathion toxicological equivalents.
Overall, the JMPR and EU residue definitions for enforcement are not comparable, JMPR proposed parent malathion only for plants and a different residue definition for animal products, whereas the EU definition includes malathion and malaoxon. For risk assessment, JMPR did not finalise the residue definition, while the EU definition includes additional toxicologically relevant metabolites.

JMPR: Sum of 2‐phenylphenol and its salts and conjugates, expressed as 2‐phenylphenol
EU: Reg. 396/2005: 2‐phenylphenol (sum of 2‐phenylphenol and its conjugates, expressed as 2‐phenylphenol)
efsa_comments:
JMPR 2025 assessed plant metabolism in oranges and pears following post‐harvest dip treatments. In both crops, residues were mainly represented by parent 2‐phenylphenol, present as free and conjugated forms and accounting for more than 80% of the TRR. Only minor metabolites, namely PHQ (2‐phenylhydroquinone) and 2‐MBP (2‐methoxybiphenyl), were identified at low levels, mainly in orange peel. Based on these data, JMPR derived the residue definition for enforcement in plant commodities as the sum of 2‐phenylphenol, its salts and conjugates, expressed as 2‐phenylphenol. However, JMPR was unable to conclude on residue definitions for risk assessment in plant and animal commodities due to the unfinalised toxicological evaluation (see table above on HBGV) and lack of validated analytical methods, in particular for conjugated residues in livestock.
At EU level, during the peer review process currently ongoing (TC 96),
15
the same fruit metabolism studies were available. Similar residue definition was proposed for enforcement, confirming the existing one. For risk assessment, the proposed residue definition was the sum of 2‐phenylphenol, its salts and conjugates, expressed as 2‐phenylphenol, whereas the existing residue definition also includes 2‐phenylhydroquinone. Although this metabolite was not included in the proposed risk assessment residue definition in the latest EFSA peer review, a data gap was identified to address its genotoxicity. It is noted that the available metabolism studies only cover post‐harvest uses; therefore, the residue definition is limited to this use pattern. Any extension to other uses would need to be supported by appropriate metabolism studies covering those uses.

EU:
Reg. 396/2005: Pyriproxyfen
MRL review (EFSA, 2022g):
Fruits, pulses/oilseeds, root and tuber (vegetables seedbeds: BBCH 00 – early post‐emergence), following foliar treatment: Pyriproxyfen

efsa_comments:
JMPR assessed plant metabolism studies in fruit crops (apples and tomatoes) and pulses/oilseeds (cotton seed) in 2000, based on which a residue definition for plants was proposed as pyriproxyfen. However, the metabolism data available for these two crop groups are not considered sufficient to support extrapolation of the residue definition for risk assessment to leafy crops.

In the MRL review, however, pyriproxyfen was authorised for feed items that might be fed to livestock and the residue definition proposed for animal commodities was pyriproxyfen.
JMPR assessed commodities of animal origin in 1999 and derived a residue definition for animal products covering also the parent compound only.

Fruit crops: Cyprodinil
Cereal/grass crops: Cyprodinil by default (provisional, pending submission of new metabolism study on cereals)

efsa_comments:
Plant products
: The residue definitions for enforcement and risk assessment derived by JMPR and at EU levels are identical.
In the framework of the renewal of the approval for cyprodinil, a new provisional residue definition for risk assessment for fruit crops was proposed: cyprodinil and CGA232449 (free and conjugated), pending submission of toxicity data on CGA232449.
In addition, a residue definition for rotational crops was proposed provisionally proposed: NOA422054 (free and conjugate), pending submission of toxicity data on NOA422054 and on documentation of the maximum storage duration and conditions of the residue samples of the available rotational crop field trials, and additional rotational crop trials measuring levels of NOA422054 and CGA321915, including conjugated residues, and covering the PEC accumulation in 20 cm of soil for cyprodinil, CGA249287 and CGA321915).
Mango is an evergreen tree and papaya a short‐lived perennial; thus, these crops would generally not be considered rotational crops according to the EFSA guidance on rotational crops (EFSA, 2023g).
Animal products:
In contrast to the JMPR, the EU residue definitions for enforcement and risk assessment include metabolite CGA304075 in either free (animal tissues) or in free and conjugated form (milk). However, the Codex MRLs are proposed at the LOQ for commodities of animal origin; therefore, the differences in residue definitions are of low importance for the consumer exposure assessment.

Reg. 396/2005 (implementing MRL review): Pyraclostrobin
Peer review (EFSA, 2025c): Pyraclostrobin
efsa_comments: JMPR and EU residue definitions for enforcement are comparable for both plant and animal commodities. For risk assessment in plant commodities, the EU peer review included metabolite 500M07 together with parent. The expression is provisional pending on the toxicity profile for metabolite 500M07. However, residue data for representative uses of the EU peer review (EFSA, 2025c) were expressed provisionally as pyraclostrobin. For animal commodities, the EU residue definition is broader than the JMPR residue definition, as it covers pyraclostrobin and its metabolites analysed as 500M04 and 500M85. For plant commodities, the Article 12 MRL review risk assessment residue definition matches the JMPR definition. However, the 2017 EU peer review proposed extending it to include three trifloxystrobin isomers. As the toxicity of these isomers and metabolite CGA 321113 has not yet been fully addressed, this residue definition is not yet fully applicable.
For animal commodities, the EU and JMPR risk assessment residue definitions are also comparable. The main difference is that the EU risk assessment residue definitions for ruminants, CGA 321113 includes both free and conjugated forms, whereas for poultry only the free form is considered.

JMPR: Cyantraniliprole
EU:
Reg. 396/2005: Cyantraniliprole
Peer review (EFSA, 2014f): Cyantraniliprole
efsa_comments:
EU plant:
Metabolism studies in four crop groups showed a similar metabolic profile across application methods, with cyantraniliprole as the main residue. Therefore, the enforcement and risk assessment RDs were proposed as cyantraniliprole.
Processed commodities:
Cyantraniliprole was stable under pasteurisation and sterilisation but degraded under boiling, mainly to IN‐J9Z38, also confirmed in processing studies. The RDs were proposed as cyantraniliprole for enforcement and the sum of cyantraniliprole and IN‐J9Z38, expressed as cyantraniliprole, for risk assessment. JMPR proposed similar RDs for plant and processed products.
EU animal:
Goat and poultry metabolism studies showed extensive excretion and limited residues in tissues, milk and eggs. The EU RD‐RA was proposed as the sum of cyantraniliprole, IN‐J9Z38, IN‐MLA84 and IN‐N7B69, expressed as cyantraniliprole, with a conversion factor of 2 except for meat and honey. JMPR assessed the same studies but also included IN‐MYX98 in the risk assessment RD, as it occurred at significant levels in muscle and milk.

Peer review (EFSA, 2018i): Mefentrifluconazole
efsa_comments:
Plant commodities
: The residue definitions for enforcement and risk assessment derived by JMPR and at EU level are identical. However, in the EU, additional risk assessment residue definitions comprising the TDMs were set.
Animal commodities:
JMPR proposed the residue definition for enforcement as mefentrifluconazole, free and conjugated, whereas the EU residue definition includes only the free form of the parent. The JMPR residue definition is not considered appropriate for EU enforcement because the individual conjugates are not sufficiently defined, analytical standards and enforcement methods are not available and the conjugates are of minor relevance. Therefore, the parent compound is considered an appropriate marker for enforcement. For risk assessment, the JMPR and EU residue definitions are not comparable, as the JMPR residue definition includes parent conjugates and M750F022, free and conjugated, whereas the EU residue definition includes M750F022 and, for poultry only, also the fatty acid conjugates of M750F022; TDMs are included separately by EU. Since feeding study samples were not analysed for conjugates, JMPR derived correction factors from metabolism studies.

JMPR:
Acequinocyl
The residue is not fat soluble
EU:
Reg. 396/2005: Acequinocyl
MRL review (EFSA, 2020a): Ruminants and swine: Acequinocyl
Peer review (EFSA, 2013f): not required
The residue is fat soluble
efsa_comments:
Metabolism studies in fruit and fruiting vegetables (orange, apple and eggplant) and hops showed a comparable pathway, with parent acequinocyl as the predominant residue (28%–95% TRR) and metabolites mainly formed by hydrolysis. The major metabolites were AKM‐05 (generally < 0.1%–4% TRR, up to 10% TRR in eggplant), AKM‐18 (≤ 7% TRR) and phthalic acid (typically ≤ 10%–17% TRR, but present at lower levels than the parent compound).
In livestock, metabolism was limited and residue transfer to tissues and milk was very low. Parent acequinocyl was detected at low levels, while metabolites AKM‐05, AKM‐15 and AKM‐18 were present only as minor components.
On this basis, JMPR established acequinocyl as the residue definition for enforcement in both plant and animal commodities. For risk assessment, the plant residue definition includes the sum of acequinocyl and AKM‐05, whereas the livestock residue definition includes acequinocyl only. Although leaves were harvested at 5 and 21 days after application (DAA), the residues were not characterised in leaves, but only in dried hop cones. Therefore, the available metabolism data should not be sufficient to support coverage of leafy crops.
At EU level, similar plant and livestock metabolism studies were assessed. The residue definitions for enforcement and risk assessment in plants and livestock include only acequinocyl, except for processed commodities, for which acequinocyl‐OH (AKM‐05) was tentatively included as a hydrolysis metabolite. EFSA requested additional standard hydrolysis studies to conclude on the relevance of this metabolite in the residue definition for processed commodities.

JMPR: Proquinazid
EU:
Reg. 396/2005 (implementing MRL review): Proquinazid
Peer review (EFSA, 2026a):
Cereals and fruit crops: Proquinazid
efsa_comments:
JMPR assessed metabolism studies in primary crops on apple, grape, and wheat. In addition, two confined rotational crops metabolism studies conducted on roots, pulses and oilseeds, leafy crops and cereals and covering all PBIs were also available.
For enforcement in plants, JMPR included proquinazid as it was the major compound in all crops assessed. For RD‐RA, JMPR considered the occurrence and toxicological relevance of the main metabolites found in the investigated crops. IN‐MW977 (isomers) was the only major metabolite in plants; JMPR considered that IM‐MW977 is covered by the HBGV of proquinazid and included in the residue definition for dietary intake.
At EU level, the same metabolism studies were assessed during the peer review and similar conclusions were reached for the residue definition for enforcement and for the inclusion of IN‐MW977 in the RD‐RA for plants. The different outcome relates to the toxicological assessment of IN‐MW977, which was not considered covered by the toxicity of the parent compound at EU level. Therefore, a data gap for general toxicity data was identified and IN‐MW977 was provisionally included in the EU RD‐RA for plants.
In livestock, JMPR assessed metabolism studies on poultry and ruminants, and a ruminant feeding study.
Based on the studies for enforcement, proquinazid and metabolite IM‐MU210 (the only compound found in ruminant feeding study) were included in the RD. Although IN‐MW977 was found in feed items, JMPR did not include it in the enforcement residue definition, as IM‐MU210 was considered the higher contributor. For the RD‐RA in animal commodities JMPR considered again the occurrence and toxicological relevance of metabolites. Metabolite IN‐MU210 was found in high levels in milk and ruminant tissues while IN‐MW977 was observed only in goat fat. In poultry, several metabolites were observed (e.g. IN‐MW977, IN‐MW398, IN‐NA250, sulfate conjugates of hydroxylated proquinazid, IN‐MY788), however their levels are expected to be low considering the level used in the metabolism study (30N); therefore, their inclusion in the RD‐RA was not deemed necessary. Based on these results, JMPR included proquinazid and IM‐MU210 in the RD‐RA for animal commodities.
At the EU level, the same livestock metabolism and feeding studies were assessed and a residue definition for enforcement comparable to that derived by JMPR was proposed. The EU RD‐RA for livestock is broader as it includes both IN‐MU210 and IN‐MW977. In the EU, the residue definitions are provisional, pending the toxicity data for metabolites IN‐MU210 and IN‐MW977 (see above toxicological information on the HBGVs table).
For metabolite CRC‐Soy‐01 which was identified at low levels in rotational crops, JMPR concluded that the threshold of toxicological concern (TTC) Cramer class III approach for chronic exposure (1.5 μg/kg bw per day) and for acute exposure (5 μg/kg bw) should be considered. For the current assessment and considering the low levels of CRC‐Soy‐01, JMPR decided that a dietary intake estimation was not necessary. However, JMPR noted, that this decision should be revisited in case future uses result in higher maximum seasonal application rates. In the EU, a data gap was set regarding the genotoxic potential and general toxicity for metabolite CRC‐Soy‐01.
